description: We’re a team of 2 from lucknow who love space and believe the best way to learn engineering is to play with it. Our team brings together and we built Outpost Commander to show kids that surviving on the Moon is about making smart trade-offs. We used real NASA data, so every storm and every choice a young commander faces comes from real science.
summary:
Outpost Zero is a browser game for children aged 7 to 12 in which they run a base on the Moon, on Mars or aboard a deep-space ship. Each day, called a sol, players split six crew members between power, air, food, shielding and science. Because there are only six people, every choice costs something, and a preview line shows the effect on power, oxygen, food and radiation before the day is run. Forecasts warn about lunar night, dust storms and solar flares, while equipment failures arrive without warning. An animated scene shows the base, the weather and the ship’s spinning ring.

The game has eleven levels, and each introduces one new idea, from power basics to air and food, radiation, lunar night, science goals, flares, Mars, storms and finally the Endurance ship, inspired by Interstellar. Every level ends with a three-question quiz. Players earn stars, badges that give perks in later missions, and three guides in a Space Library: Beginner, Intermediate and Advanced. Everything stays locked until a player creates an account with a name and a four-digit PIN, or logs in, and progress is saved for each account.

The science is grounded in real data. The solar flares come from NASA’s DONKI records, and the radiation levels and radio delays are real measurements. The flare list is archived rather than live, and the game says so. Other numbers, such as oxygen and food, are simplified for play.
details:
Outpost Zero: project details

What does it do and how does it work?

Outpost Zero is a browser game for children aged 7 to 12. Players run a base on the Moon, on Mars or aboard a deep-space ship.

  • Daily decisions: each day (a “sol”) the player splits six crew between power, air, food, shielding and science. There are only six people, so every choice costs something.
  • Visible trade-offs: a preview line shows the expected change in power, oxygen, food and radiation before the player commits.
  • Events: a forecast warns about lunar night, dust storms and solar flares. Equipment failures arrive without warning.
  • Communication delay: on the Moon, Earth helps in about 3 seconds. On Mars and on the ship, the crew must fix problems alone.
  • Campaign: eleven levels each introduce one new idea and get harder, ending with the Endurance ship mission, a spinning-ring ship inspired by Interstellar.
  • Learning loop: every level ends with a 3-question quiz. Players earn stars and badges that give perks in later missions. They also unlock three guides (Beginner, Intermediate and Advanced) in a Space Library.
  • Accounts: everything is locked until a player creates an account with a name and 4-digit PIN, or logs in. Progress is saved per account.
  • Visuals: an animated scene shows the base, weather, flares, astronauts and the ship’s spinning ring.

What benefits does it have?

  • Players learn real constraints by making decisions, not by reading facts.
  • It needs no download and runs in a browser.
  • It uses plain language and explains terms where they appear, such as sol, radiation and mSv.
  • Failure explains itself, so replaying feels like learning, not punishment.
  • The guides, quizzes and levels give a path from beginner to advanced ideas, and it can work for older siblings, parents or a classroom.

What is the intended impact?

We want a young player to leave understanding that deep-space survival is about balancing limited crew time, power, air, food and radiation protection. We also want them to see that real NASA data shapes those choices, and to be curious enough to explore the guides and NASA’s data themselves.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages and technology: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with an HTML canvas for the animated scene and the browser’s local storage for accounts. The page is a single file with no framework.
  • Platform: the game is published as a claude.ai artifact. When the page is opened signed in, claude.ai’s built-in database and user features add account syncing across devices.
  • AI assistant: we built it with Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, which wrote the code, text and guides.
  • Testing: scripted playtests in Node.js with the jsdom library, plus a simple bot to check difficulty.
  • Presentation: a PowerPoint deck made with the pptxgenjs library.
  • Hardware: nothing special. It runs on any device with a modern browser.

NASA data used

  • Each solar flare in the game is a real one from NASA’s DONKI space-weather records: X5.8 (11 May 2024), X9.0 (3 Oct 2024), X9.3 (6 Sep 2017) and X17 (28 Oct 2003). This is an archived list built into the game, not a live feed, and the game says so.
  • Radiation per day is about 0.7 mSv on Mars (NASA’s Curiosity rover) and about 1.4 mSv on the Moon (Chang’e-4 lander measurements).
  • Radio delay is 1.3 seconds to the Moon and 4 to 24 minutes to Mars.
  • Oxygen, food, power and crew numbers are invented for play.
  • I wrote the dates, figures and guide facts from memory, so please check them against the NASA sources before you submit.

How is it creative?

  • It turns real mission constraints into a game with only a few numbers, instead of a long simulation.
  • The expected-change preview makes the cost of every choice visible before the player commits.
  • Radio delay changes gameplay: the same breakdown is easy to fix on the Moon but deadly on Mars.
  • The campaign teaches one new idea per level, then ends with an Interstellar-inspired ship mission featuring artificial gravity, a dark passage past a black hole and far-away power problems.
  • Real solar flares, quizzes, perks and an animated scene keep it engaging and replayable.

What factors did we consider?

  • Audience: kids aged 7 to 12, so few simultaneous systems, plain language and no jargon without explanation.
  • No free choice: every decision costs something, so we tested that doing nothing loses.
  • Difficulty: we tuned levels with a bot so early levels are gentle and later ones are hard. We have not tested with real children.
  • Honesty about data: we label archived data as archived and invented numbers as simplified.
  • Accessibility: a reduced-motion setting is respected, and buttons are keyboard-friendly.
  • Safety and privacy: accounts use a name and PIN only, with no email. The PIN gives only basic protection and the game warns players not to reuse a real PIN.
  • Limits we know about: we did not test on a real phone or with the claude.ai sync, and the locking can be bypassed by a technically skilled player.
